questions.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $C$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=10$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $C,$ then $C$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $C=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $C,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
C={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}10 & 15 \\ 20 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -2 & 11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $A$, then  $A$ must be diagonalizable. 

So, we can write $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $A$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain,

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 15 \\ 4 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $E$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $E,$ then $E$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $E=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $E,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
E={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}E & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}12 & 12 \\ 16 & 24\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $G$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $G,$ then $G$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $G=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $G,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
G={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}G & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-16 & 9 \\ -30 & 17\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
